groups.title: Govern
groups.description: The organization's cybersecurity risk management strategy, expectations, and policy are established, communicated, and monitored

groups.title: Organizational Context
groups.description: The circumstances - mission, stakeholder expectations, dependencies, and legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements - surrounding the organization's cybersecurity risk management decisions are understood

groups.title: Risk Management Strategy
groups.description: The organization's priorities, constraints, risk tolerance and appetite statements, and assumptions are established, communicated, and used to support operational risk decisions

groups.title: Roles, Responsibilities, and Authorities
groups.description: Cybersecurity roles, responsibilities, and authorities to foster accountability, performance assessment, and continuous improvement are established and communicated

groups.title: Policy
groups.description: Organizational cybersecurity policy is established, communicated, and enforced

groups.title: Oversight
groups.description: Results of organization-wide cybersecurity risk management activities and performance are used to inform, improve, and adjust the risk management strategy

groups.title: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management
groups.description: Cyber supply chain risk management processes are identified, established, managed, monitored, and improved by organizational stakeholders

groups.title: Identify
groups.description: The organization's current cybersecurity risks are understood

groups.title: Asset Management
groups.description: Assets (e.g., data, hardware, software, systems, facilities, services, people) that enable the organization to achieve business purposes are identified and managed consistent with their relative importance to organizational objectives and the organization's risk strategy

groups.title: Risk Assessment
groups.description: The cybersecurity risk to the organization, assets, and individuals is understood by the organization

groups.title: Improvement
groups.description: Improvements to organizational cybersecurity risk management processes, procedures and activities are identified across all CSF Functions

groups.title: Protect
groups.description: Safeguards to manage the organization's cybersecurity risks are used

groups.title: Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control
groups.description: Access to physical and logical assets is limited to authorized users, services, and hardware and managed commensurate with the assessed risk of unauthorized access

groups.title: Awareness and Training
groups.description: The organization's personnel are provided with cybersecurity awareness and training so that they can perform their cybersecurity-related tasks

groups.title: Data Security
groups.description: Data are managed consistent with the organization's risk strategy to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information

groups.title: Platform Security
groups.description: The hardware, software (e.g., firmware, operating systems, applications), and services of physical and virtual platforms are managed consistent with the organization's risk strategy to protect their confidentiality, integrity, and availability

groups.title: Technology Infrastructure Resilience
groups.description: Security architectures are managed with the organization's risk strategy to protect asset confidentiality, integrity, and availability, and organizational resilience

groups.title: Detect
groups.description: Possible cybersecurity attacks and compromises are found and analyzed

groups.title: Adverse Event Analysis
groups.description: Anomalies, indicators of compromise, and other potentially adverse events are analyzed to characterize the events and detect cybersecurity incidents

groups.title: Continuous Monitoring
groups.description: Assets are monitored to find anomalies, indicators of compromise, and other potentially adverse events

groups.title: Respond
groups.description: Actions regarding a detected cybersecurity incident are taken

groups.title: Incident Management
groups.description: Responses to detected cybersecurity incidents are managed

groups.title: Incident Analysis
groups.description: Investigations are conducted to ensure effective response and support forensics and recovery activities

groups.title: Incident Response Reporting and Communication
groups.description: Response activities are coordinated with internal and external stakeholders as required by laws, regulations, or policies

groups.title: Incident Mitigation
groups.description: Activities are performed to prevent expansion of an event and mitigate its effects

groups.title: Recover
groups.description: Assets and operations affected by a cybersecurity incident are restored

groups.title: Incident Recovery Plan Execution
groups.description: Restoration activities are performed to ensure operational availability of systems and services affected by cybersecurity incidents

groups.title: Incident Recovery Communication
groups.description: Restoration activities are coordinated with internal and external parties

requirements.title: The organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management

statement.text: The organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Share the organization's mission (e.g., through vision and mission statements, marketing, and service strategies) to provide a basis for identifying risks that may impede that mission

editorial.question: Does your organization's understanding of its mission, and what it must keep delivering, shape how you decide which cybersecurity risks matter most?
editorial.whyItMatters: Security decisions made without reference to the mission tend to protect the wrong things or spread effort evenly across everything. Knowing what the organization exists to do shows which disruptions would hurt most.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Your mission is written down and shared, for example in a mission statement or service strategy, and the people who manage cybersecurity risk use it as the basis for identifying risks that could get in the way of that mission.
nextSteps: Write a short statement of what your organization does and for whom, or locate the one you already have.
List the few activities that would most directly stop you delivering that mission if they were disrupted.
Share the mission statement with whoever makes security and technology decisions, and refer to it when ranking risks.

requirements.title: Internal and external stakeholders are understood, and their needs and expectations regarding cybersecurity risk management are understood and considered

statement.text: Internal and external stakeholders are understood, and their needs and expectations regarding cybersecurity risk management are understood and considered

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Identify relevant internal stakeholders and their cybersecurity-related expectations (e.g., performance and risk expectations of officers, directors, and advisors; cultural expectations of employees)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify relevant external stakeholders and their cybersecurity-related expectations (e.g., privacy expectations of customers, business expectations of partnerships, compliance expectations of regulators, ethics expectations of society)

editorial.question: Does your organization know who its internal and external stakeholders are and what each expects from you on cybersecurity, and take those expectations into account?
editorial.whyItMatters: Customers, partners, regulators, owners, and staff each expect different things, such as privacy for customer data or reliability for a partner. Missing one of these expectations can cost trust, contracts, or penalties even when nothing has been breached.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have identified internal stakeholders (such as owners, directors, advisors, and employees) and external stakeholders (such as customers, partners, regulators, and the wider community), along with their cybersecurity and privacy expectations, and those expectations are considered when you set priorities.
nextSteps: List the groups inside and outside the organization who rely on or oversee how you handle security.
Write down what each group expects, for example customer privacy, partner reliability, or regulator reporting.
Review the list when you set security priorities, and update it when you gain a major customer, partner, or regulator.

requirements.title: Legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements regarding cybersecurity - including privacy and civil liberties obligations - are understood and managed

statement.text: Legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements regarding cybersecurity - including privacy and civil liberties obligations - are understood and managed

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Determine a process to track and manage legal and regulatory requirements regarding protection of individuals' information (e.g., Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, California Consumer Privacy Act, General Data Protection Regulation)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Determine a process to track and manage contractual requirements for cybersecurity management of supplier, customer, and partner information

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Align the organization's cybersecurity strategy with legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements

editorial.question: Does your organization know which laws, regulations, and contract terms set cybersecurity or privacy obligations for you, and have a way to track and meet them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Privacy laws, industry regulations, and customer contracts often carry specific security duties and breach notification rules. Missing one can lead to fines, lost contracts, or harm to the people whose information you hold.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You keep a current record of the legal, regulatory, and contractual cybersecurity requirements that apply to you, including privacy obligations that protect individuals' information and security terms in supplier, customer, and partner agreements. Someone tracks changes to these requirements, and your cybersecurity strategy is aligned with them.
nextSteps: List the privacy and security laws that apply to you based on where you operate and the kinds of personal information you hold, such as health or consumer data.
Review your customer, supplier, and partner contracts for security and data handling clauses, and record them in one place.
Assign someone to watch for new or changed requirements and report them to leadership.
Check that your security plans address each requirement on the list.

requirements.title: Critical objectives, capabilities, and services that external stakeholders depend on or expect from the organization are understood and communicated

statement.text: Critical objectives, capabilities, and services that external stakeholders depend on or expect from the organization are understood and communicated

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish criteria for determining the criticality of capabilities and services as viewed by internal and external stakeholders

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Determine (e.g., from a business impact analysis) assets and business operations that are vital to achieving mission objectives and the potential impact of a loss (or partial loss) of such operations

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Establish and communicate resilience objectives (e.g., recovery time objectives) for delivering critical capabilities and services in various operating states (e.g., under attack, during recovery, normal operation)

editorial.question: Does your organization know which of its services and capabilities customers and partners depend on most, and has that been communicated to the people who need to know?
editorial.whyItMatters: When something goes wrong, you need to know which services to protect and restore first. Customers and partners who rely on you also need to know what to expect during an outage or attack.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have criteria for deciding which capabilities and services are critical, an understanding of the assets and operations they depend on and the impact of losing them (often from a business impact analysis), and resilience objectives, such as how long a service can be down, that you have communicated for normal operation, during an attack, and during recovery.
nextSteps: List the services customers and partners rely on you for, and rank them by the harm an outage would cause.
Identify the systems, data, and people each critical service needs in order to run.
Set a target for how quickly each critical service must be restored and how it should operate during an attack or recovery.
Share these priorities and targets with the staff who run the services and, where appropriate, with key customers.

requirements.title: Outcomes, capabilities, and services that the organization depends on are understood and communicated

statement.text: Outcomes, capabilities, and services that the organization depends on are understood and communicated

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Create an inventory of the organization's dependencies on external resources (e.g., facilities, cloud-based hosting providers) and their relationships to organizational assets and business functions

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify and document external dependencies that are potential points of failure for the organization's critical capabilities and services, and share that information with appropriate personnel

editorial.question: Does your organization know which outside services and resources it depends on, such as cloud hosting, internet, or facilities, and is that shared with the right people?
editorial.whyItMatters: Most organizations rely on providers they do not control, such as a hosting provider, payment processor, or building landlord. If one fails, your own services can stop, so knowing these points of failure lets you plan around them.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You keep an inventory of external dependencies, such as facilities and cloud hosting providers, showing which assets and business functions rely on each. Dependencies that could become single points of failure for critical services are documented and shared with the people who need to plan for them.
nextSteps: List the outside providers and resources your daily operations rely on, including internet, power, cloud services, and key vendors.
Note which business functions and systems would stop if each one failed.
Flag the dependencies that have no backup or alternative, and share that list with the people responsible for continuity planning.

requirements.title: Risk management objectives are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders

statement.text: Risk management objectives are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Update near-term and long-term cybersecurity risk management objectives as part of annual strategic planning and when major changes occur

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Establish measurable objectives for cybersecurity risk management (e.g., manage the quality of user training, ensure adequate risk protection for industrial control systems)

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Senior leaders agree about cybersecurity objectives and use them for measuring and managing risk and performance

editorial.question: Has your organization set cybersecurity risk management objectives that leadership has agreed to and uses to measure progress?
editorial.whyItMatters: Without agreed objectives, security work drifts toward whatever is urgent or interesting rather than what the organization needs. Objectives that leadership has signed off on also make it clearer where to spend and whether efforts are working.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have written, measurable cybersecurity risk management objectives, both near term and long term, such as a target for the quality of staff training. Senior leaders agree on them, use them to measure and manage risk and performance, and update them during annual strategic planning and when major changes occur.
nextSteps: Draft a few cybersecurity objectives tied to your business goals, each with a way to measure it.
Review the draft with the owners or senior leaders and agree on a final version.
Add a review of these objectives to your annual planning cycle and to your response to any major change in the business.

requirements.title: Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated, and maintained

statement.text: Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated, and maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Determine and communicate risk appetite statements that convey expectations about the appropriate level of risk for the organization

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Translate risk appetite statements into specific, measurable, and broadly understandable risk tolerance statements

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Refine organizational objectives and risk appetite periodically based on known risk exposure and residual risk

editorial.question: Has your organization stated how much cybersecurity risk it is willing to accept, and turned that into specific, measurable limits people understand?
editorial.whyItMatters: Without a shared view of acceptable risk, people make inconsistent calls, accepting serious risks in one area while overspending on minor ones elsewhere. Clear limits let staff make routine decisions without escalating every question.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Leadership has written risk appetite statements (the broad level of risk the organization is willing to take on) and translated them into risk tolerance statements (specific, measurable limits, such as the longest acceptable outage for a key system). These are communicated to the people who make risk decisions and refined periodically based on known exposure and remaining risk.
nextSteps: Discuss with leadership which kinds of cybersecurity risk the organization will and will not accept, and write it down in a few sentences.
Turn each statement into a measurable limit that staff can apply, such as acceptable downtime or data loss for a key system.
Share the statements with the people who make technology and security decisions.
Set a time to revisit them, for example during annual planning.

requirements.title: Cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes

statement.text: Cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Aggregate and manage cybersecurity risks alongside other enterprise risks (e.g., compliance, financial, operational, regulatory, reputational, safety)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Include cybersecurity risk managers in enterprise risk management planning

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Establish criteria for escalating cybersecurity risks within enterprise risk management

editorial.question: Are cybersecurity risks tracked and managed alongside your organization's other business risks, such as financial, legal, operational, and reputational risks?
editorial.whyItMatters: When cybersecurity is handled separately, leaders cannot weigh it against other risks competing for the same money and attention. Bringing it into the same process helps serious cyber risks reach the people who decide.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Cybersecurity risks are aggregated and managed in the same process used for other enterprise risks, the people who manage cybersecurity risk take part in enterprise risk planning, and there are defined criteria for when a cybersecurity risk is escalated.
nextSteps: Add your main cybersecurity risks to the list or process you use for other business risks, or start one if none exists.
Include whoever manages cybersecurity in business risk and planning discussions.
Agree on the conditions under which a cybersecurity risk must be raised with owners or senior leaders.

requirements.title: Strategic direction that describes appropriate risk response options is established and communicated

statement.text: Strategic direction that describes appropriate risk response options is established and communicated

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Specify criteria for accepting and avoiding cybersecurity risk for various classifications of data

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Determine whether to purchase cybersecurity insurance

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Document conditions under which shared responsibility models are acceptable (e.g., outsourcing certain cybersecurity functions, having a third party perform financial transactions on behalf of the organization, using public cloud-based services)

editorial.question: Has your organization decided and communicated how it will respond to different kinds of cybersecurity risk, such as which risks to accept, avoid, insure, or share with providers?
editorial.whyItMatters: Not every risk can or should be fixed. Clear direction on when to accept, avoid, transfer, or reduce a risk keeps decisions consistent and makes choices like buying insurance or outsourcing deliberate rather than accidental.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have documented criteria for accepting or avoiding cybersecurity risk for different classifications of data, a decision on whether to buy cybersecurity insurance, and the conditions under which shared responsibility arrangements are acceptable, such as outsourcing security functions, having a third party perform financial transactions for you, or using public cloud services. This direction is communicated to the people who make those decisions.
nextSteps: Group your data by sensitivity and write down which risks you will accept or avoid for each group.
Decide whether cybersecurity insurance makes sense for your organization, and record the reasoning.
Write down when it is acceptable to rely on a provider for part of your security, such as cloud hosting or a managed security service.
Share this guidance with anyone who signs up for services or approves technology purchases.

requirements.title: Lines of communication across the organization are established for cybersecurity risks, including risks from suppliers and other third parties

statement.text: Lines of communication across the organization are established for cybersecurity risks, including risks from suppliers and other third parties

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Determine how to update senior executives, directors, and management on the organization's cybersecurity posture at agreed-upon intervals

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify how all departments across the organization - such as management, operations, internal auditors, legal, acquisition, physical security, and HR - will communicate with each other about cybersecurity risks

editorial.question: Are there clear, agreed ways for people across your organization to raise and share cybersecurity risks, including risks that come from suppliers and other third parties?
editorial.whyItMatters: Risks often surface in one part of an organization, such as purchasing, HR, or facilities, while the people who can act on them sit elsewhere. Defined lines of communication help these concerns reach leadership and the right teams in time.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have defined how and at what intervals senior executives, directors, and managers are updated on cybersecurity posture, and how departments such as operations, legal, purchasing, HR, physical security, and any internal audit function communicate with each other about cybersecurity risks, including supplier and third-party risks.
nextSteps: Agree how often, and in what form, leadership will receive a cybersecurity update.
Name a contact in each department for raising cybersecurity concerns, and tell staff who it is.
Make sure the people who buy services or manage vendors know where to report supplier security concerns.

requirements.title: A standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing, and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated

statement.text: A standardized method for calculating, documenting, categorizing, and prioritizing cybersecurity risks is established and communicated

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish criteria for using a quantitative approach to cybersecurity risk analysis, and specify probability and exposure formulas

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Create and use templates (e.g., a risk register) to document cybersecurity risk information (e.g., risk description, exposure, treatment, and ownership)

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Establish criteria for risk prioritization at the appropriate levels within the enterprise

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Use a consistent list of risk categories to support integrating, aggregating, and comparing cybersecurity risks

editorial.question: Does your organization use a consistent method to assess, record, categorize, and rank cybersecurity risks, and do the people involved know how to use it?
editorial.whyItMatters: If each person rates risk differently, risks cannot be compared and the most serious ones may not get attention first. A shared method makes risk decisions repeatable and easier to explain.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have a documented way to calculate cybersecurity risk, whether with rating scales or numeric formulas, a standard template such as a risk register (a list of risks with their description, exposure, treatment, and owner), a consistent set of risk categories, and criteria for prioritizing risks at the right level of the organization. The method has been shared with the people who use it.
nextSteps: Choose a rating approach, such as scoring likelihood and impact on a fixed scale, and write it down.
Create a risk register with columns for the risk, its rating, category, owner, and planned treatment.
Define a short list of risk categories and the rating at which a risk must be escalated.
Walk the people who record or review risks through the method.

requirements.title: Strategic opportunities (i.e., positive risks) are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions

statement.text: Strategic opportunities (i.e., positive risks) are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Define and communicate guidance and methods for identifying opportunities and including them in risk discussions (e.g., strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify stretch goals and document them

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Calculate, document, and prioritize positive risks alongside negative risks

editorial.question: When your organization discusses cybersecurity risk, does it also identify and weigh opportunities, such as ways security could support new business or better services?
editorial.whyItMatters: Risk is not only about what could go wrong. Recognizing positive risks, such as a security capability that helps win customers or enables a new service, helps leaders balance protection with growth instead of treating security only as a cost.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have guidance and methods for identifying opportunities (positive risks) and including them in risk discussions, for example an analysis of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Stretch goals are documented, and opportunities are calculated, documented, and prioritized alongside negative risks.
nextSteps: Add a standing question about opportunities to your risk reviews, such as where security improvements could help win work or enable new services.
Use a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats exercise during planning to surface positive risks.
Record promising opportunities and stretch goals in your risk register and rank them alongside other risks.

requirements.title: Organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical, and continually improving

statement.text: Organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical, and continually improving

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Leaders (e.g., directors) agree on their roles and responsibilities in developing, implementing, and assessing the organization's cybersecurity strategy

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Share leaders' expectations regarding a secure and ethical culture, especially when current events present the opportunity to highlight positive or negative examples of cybersecurity risk management

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Leaders direct the CISO to maintain a comprehensive cybersecurity risk strategy and review and update it at least annually and after major events

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Conduct reviews to ensure adequate authority and coordination among those responsible for managing cybersecurity risk

editorial.question: Do your organization's leaders take responsibility for cybersecurity risk and actively encourage a culture that is risk-aware, ethical, and continually improving?
editorial.whyItMatters: Staff take their cues from leadership. When owners and senior leaders treat cybersecurity as their own responsibility, it gets resources and attention, and people are more willing to report mistakes and concerns.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Leaders have agreed on their roles in developing, implementing, and assessing the cybersecurity strategy, and they share expectations for a secure and ethical culture, for example by discussing relevant current events. They direct whoever leads cybersecurity to maintain a risk strategy that is reviewed at least annually and after major events, and they check that those responsible have enough authority and coordination.
nextSteps: Agree among owners or senior leaders who is accountable for cybersecurity risk and what each leader's role is.
Have leaders talk about security expectations in staff meetings, using real-world incidents as examples.
Ask whoever leads cybersecurity to maintain a written risk strategy, and review it with leadership at least once a year and after major events.

requirements.title: Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood, and enforced

statement.text: Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood, and enforced

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Document risk management roles and responsibilities in policy

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Document who is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk management activities and how those teams and individuals are to be consulted and informed

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Include cybersecurity responsibilities and performance requirements in personnel descriptions

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Document performance goals for personnel with cybersecurity risk management responsibilities, and periodically measure performance to identify areas for improvement

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Clearly articulate cybersecurity responsibilities within operations, risk functions, and internal audit functions

editorial.question: Has your organization defined who is responsible for which cybersecurity risk management tasks, and do those people understand their roles and act on them?
editorial.whyItMatters: When responsibilities are vague, important tasks fall through the cracks because everyone assumes someone else is handling them. Clear roles also give people the authority to act when it matters.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Cybersecurity risk management roles, responsibilities, and authorities are documented in policy, including who is responsible, who is accountable, and who must be consulted or informed. Responsibilities appear in job descriptions, people in these roles have performance goals that are measured periodically, responsibilities within operations, risk, and any internal audit function are spelled out, and the roles are enforced.
nextSteps: List the main cybersecurity tasks, such as managing accounts, applying updates, and handling incidents, and assign an owner to each.
Record who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed for each task in a chart.
Add cybersecurity duties to relevant job descriptions and performance reviews.
Share the assignments so everyone knows whom to go to.

requirements.title: Adequate resources are allocated commensurate with the cybersecurity risk strategy, roles, responsibilities, and policies

statement.text: Adequate resources are allocated commensurate with the cybersecurity risk strategy, roles, responsibilities, and policies

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Conduct periodic management reviews to ensure that those given cybersecurity risk management responsibilities have the necessary authority

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify resource allocation and investment in line with risk tolerance and response

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Provide adequate and sufficient people, process, and technical resources to support the cybersecurity strategy

editorial.question: Does your organization provide enough people, time, money, and tools to carry out its cybersecurity strategy, roles, and policies?
editorial.whyItMatters: A strategy or policy without resources behind it is unlikely to be carried out. Matching resources to your risks helps avoid both underfunding critical protections and overspending on low-priority areas.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Resource allocation and investment decisions reflect your risk tolerance and planned risk responses. People, processes, and technology are sufficient to support the cybersecurity strategy, and management periodically reviews whether those with cybersecurity responsibilities have the authority they need.
nextSteps: Compare the tasks in your security strategy and policies with the people, time, and budget currently assigned to them.
Identify gaps where important work is unfunded or unowned, and decide whether to fund, outsource, or accept each one.
Schedule a periodic management review of cybersecurity resources and authority.

requirements.title: Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices

statement.text: Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Integrate cybersecurity risk management considerations into human resources processes (e.g., personnel screening, onboarding, change notification, offboarding)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Consider cybersecurity knowledge to be a positive factor in hiring, training, and retention decisions

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Conduct background checks prior to onboarding new personnel for sensitive roles, and periodically repeat background checks for personnel with such roles

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Define and enforce obligations for personnel to be aware of, adhere to, and uphold security policies as they relate to their roles

editorial.question: Is cybersecurity built into your human resources practices, such as screening, onboarding, role changes, and offboarding of staff?
editorial.whyItMatters: People's access and responsibilities change as they join, move, and leave. Building security into HR steps prevents gaps such as former staff keeping access or new hires not knowing the rules.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Cybersecurity is part of HR processes for screening, onboarding, change notification, and offboarding. Background checks are done before onboarding people into sensitive roles and repeated periodically, cybersecurity knowledge counts in hiring, training, and retention decisions, and staff obligations to follow security policies relevant to their roles are defined and enforced.
nextSteps: Add security steps to your onboarding and offboarding checklists, such as policy acknowledgment and removal of access.
Make sure HR notifies whoever manages access when someone changes roles or leaves.
Decide which roles are sensitive and require background checks before hiring and at intervals you define.
Include following security policies in role expectations and in your disciplinary process.

requirements.title: Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy, and priorities and is communicated and enforced

statement.text: Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy, and priorities and is communicated and enforced

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Create, disseminate, and maintain an understandable, usable risk management policy with statements of management intent, expectations, and direction

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Periodically review policy and supporting processes and procedures to ensure that they align with risk management strategy objectives and priorities, as well as the high-level direction of the cybersecurity policy

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Require approval from senior management on policy

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Communicate cybersecurity risk management policy and supporting processes and procedures across the organization

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Require personnel to acknowledge receipt of policy when first hired, annually, and whenever policy is updated

editorial.question: Does your organization have a written cybersecurity policy, approved by leadership and based on your priorities, that staff know about and are expected to follow?
editorial.whyItMatters: A policy sets out what leadership expects and gives staff a reference for everyday decisions. Without one, security practices depend on individual habits and are hard to enforce.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have an understandable cybersecurity risk management policy that states management's intent, expectations, and direction and reflects your context, strategy, and priorities. Senior management has approved it, it is communicated across the organization with its supporting procedures, staff acknowledge receiving it (for example when hired, each year, and after updates), it is reviewed periodically, and it is enforced.
nextSteps: Write a short policy covering your main security expectations, such as passwords, device use, data handling, and reporting incidents.
Have the owner or senior management formally approve it.
Share it with all staff and ask each person to confirm they have read it.
Explain what happens when the policy is not followed, and apply that consistently.

requirements.title: Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated, and enforced to reflect changes in requirements, threats, technology, and organizational mission

statement.text: Policy for managing cybersecurity risks is reviewed, updated, communicated, and enforced to reflect changes in requirements, threats, technology, and organizational mission

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Update policy based on periodic reviews of cybersecurity risk management results to ensure that policy and supporting processes and procedures adequately maintain risk at an acceptable level

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Provide a timeline for reviewing changes to the organization's risk environment (e.g., changes in risk or in the organization's mission objectives), and communicate recommended policy updates

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Update policy to reflect changes in legal and regulatory requirements

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Update policy to reflect changes in technology (e.g., adoption of artificial intelligence) and changes to the business (e.g., acquisition of a new business, new contract requirements)

editorial.question: Does your organization review and update its cybersecurity policy when laws, threats, technology, or the business change, and share the updated version with staff?
editorial.whyItMatters: A policy written for last year's tools and risks can leave new technology, such as artificial intelligence services, or new contracts unaddressed. Regular updates keep the policy relevant and enforceable.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You review the policy on a timeline you define and when the risk environment changes, and you update it based on risk management results and on changes in legal and regulatory requirements, technology, and the business, such as an acquisition or new contract terms. Updated versions are communicated and enforced.
nextSteps: Set a review schedule for your policy and note the date of the last review.
List the events that should trigger an early review, such as adopting a new technology, signing a new type of contract, or a change in law.
Record what changed in each version and notify staff of updates.

requirements.title: Cybersecurity risk management strategy outcomes are reviewed to inform and adjust strategy and direction

statement.text: Cybersecurity risk management strategy outcomes are reviewed to inform and adjust strategy and direction

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Measure how well the risk management strategy and risk results have helped leaders make decisions and achieve organizational objectives

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Examine whether cybersecurity risk strategies that impede operations or innovation should be adjusted

editorial.question: Does your organization review the results of its cybersecurity risk management strategy and use what it learns to adjust its direction?
editorial.whyItMatters: A strategy that is never checked can keep costing money and slowing work without delivering the protection it promised. Reviewing outcomes shows what is working and where to change course.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Leadership periodically assesses how well the cybersecurity risk strategy and its results have helped them make decisions and achieve organizational objectives, and examines whether security measures that get in the way of operations or innovation should be adjusted. The strategy is changed where the review shows a need.
nextSteps: Set a regular time, for example once a year, for leadership to review the results of the cybersecurity strategy.
Ask whether recent security decisions helped the business meet its objectives, and gather examples.
Ask staff where security measures slow down work, and decide whether those measures should change.

requirements.title: The cybersecurity risk management strategy is reviewed and adjusted to ensure coverage of organizational requirements and risks

statement.text: The cybersecurity risk management strategy is reviewed and adjusted to ensure coverage of organizational requirements and risks

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Review audit findings to confirm whether the existing cybersecurity strategy has ensured compliance with internal and external requirements

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Review the performance oversight of those in cybersecurity-related roles to determine whether policy changes are necessary

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Review strategy in light of cybersecurity incidents

editorial.question: Does your organization periodically check that its cybersecurity risk management strategy still covers all of its requirements and risks, and adjust it when gaps appear?
editorial.whyItMatters: Requirements and risks change as the business grows, contracts change, and incidents happen. Reviewing coverage catches gaps before an auditor, customer, or attacker finds them.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You review audit findings to confirm whether the strategy has kept you in line with internal and external requirements, review oversight of people in cybersecurity roles to see whether policy changes are needed, and revisit the strategy in light of cybersecurity incidents. The strategy is adjusted when gaps are found.
nextSteps: Compare your strategy with your list of legal, contractual, and internal requirements, and note anything not covered.
Review findings from any audits, assessments, or customer security questionnaires for gaps.
After each significant incident, ask whether the strategy needs to change and record the decision.

requirements.title: Organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed

statement.text: Organizational cybersecurity risk management performance is evaluated and reviewed for adjustments needed

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Review key performance indicators (KPIs) to ensure that organization-wide policies and procedures achieve objectives

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Review key risk indicators (KRIs) to identify risks the organization faces, including likelihood and potential impact

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Collect and communicate metrics on cybersecurity risk management with senior leadership

editorial.question: Does your organization measure how well its cybersecurity risk management is performing and review those measures to decide what to change?
editorial.whyItMatters: Without measures, it is hard to know whether security is improving or slipping. Metrics give leadership a factual basis for adjusting priorities and resources.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You review key performance indicators (measures of whether policies and procedures are achieving their objectives, such as training completion) and key risk indicators (signals of the risks you face and their likelihood and impact). These metrics are shared with senior leadership and used to identify needed adjustments.
nextSteps: Pick a handful of measures that show how security is working, such as time to apply critical updates or the share of staff trained.
Collect them on a schedule you define and report them to leadership.
Review trends with leadership and agree on adjustments when measures move the wrong way.

requirements.title: A cybersecurity supply chain risk management program, strategy, objectives, policies, and processes are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders

statement.text: A cybersecurity supply chain risk management program, strategy, objectives, policies, and processes are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish a strategy that expresses the objectives of the cybersecurity supply chain risk management program

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Develop the cybersecurity supply chain risk management program, including a plan (with milestones), policies, and procedures that guide implementation and improvement of the program, and share the policies and procedures with the organizational stakeholders

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Develop and implement program processes based on the strategy, objectives, policies, and procedures that are agreed upon and performed by the organizational stakeholders

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Establish a cross-organizational mechanism that ensures alignment between functions that contribute to cybersecurity supply chain risk management, such as cybersecurity, IT, operations, legal, human resources, and engineering

editorial.question: Has your organization set up an agreed approach, including goals, policies, and processes, for managing cybersecurity risks that come from suppliers and the wider supply chain?
editorial.whyItMatters: Many breaches start at a vendor, software provider, or service partner. A defined approach makes sure supplier risks are handled deliberately rather than case by case, and that everyone who buys and manages suppliers works the same way.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have a cybersecurity supply chain risk management program (your organized approach to supplier-related security risk) with a strategy and objectives, a plan with milestones, and policies and procedures that stakeholders have agreed to, follow, and use to improve the program. Functions such as IT, security, operations, legal, HR, and engineering stay aligned through a defined cross-organizational mechanism.
nextSteps: Write down what you want to achieve in managing supplier security risk, such as knowing which vendors hold your data.
Draft a short policy and procedure for evaluating, contracting with, and monitoring suppliers.
Agree on the approach with the people who buy, use, and manage suppliers, and set milestones for putting it in place.
Set up a regular check-in between the functions involved, such as IT, legal, and operations.

requirements.title: Cybersecurity roles and responsibilities for suppliers, customers, and partners are established, communicated, and coordinated internally and externally

statement.text: Cybersecurity roles and responsibilities for suppliers, customers, and partners are established, communicated, and coordinated internally and externally

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Identify one or more specific roles or positions that will be responsible and accountable for planning, resourcing, and executing cybersecurity supply chain risk management activities

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Document cybersecurity supply chain risk management roles and responsibilities in policy

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Create responsibility matrixes to document who will be responsible and accountable for cybersecurity supply chain risk management activities and how those teams and individuals will be consulted and informed

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Include cybersecurity supply chain risk management responsibilities and performance requirements in personnel descriptions to ensure clarity and improve accountability

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Document performance goals for personnel with cybersecurity risk management-specific responsibilities, and periodically measure them to demonstrate and improve performance

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Develop roles and responsibilities for suppliers, customers, and business partners to address shared responsibilities for applicable cybersecurity risks, and integrate them into organizational policies and applicable third-party agreements

examples.label: Ex7
examples.text: Internally communicate cybersecurity supply chain risk management roles and responsibilities for third parties

examples.label: Ex8
examples.text: Establish rules and protocols for information sharing and reporting processes between the organization and its suppliers

editorial.question: Has your organization defined and communicated the cybersecurity roles and responsibilities of its own staff, suppliers, customers, and partners for managing supply chain risks?
editorial.whyItMatters: Security gaps often appear where one party assumes the other is responsible, such as who patches a hosted system or who reports a breach. Clear roles on both sides prevent these gaps.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Specific people are responsible and accountable for supply chain risk management, as recorded in policy, a responsibility matrix, job descriptions, and measured performance goals. Shared security responsibilities with suppliers, customers, and partners are defined and written into policies and agreements, communicated internally, and supported by rules for information sharing and reporting between you and your suppliers.
nextSteps: Name who in your organization is responsible for supplier security risk.
For each key supplier, write down which security tasks are theirs and which are yours.
Add those responsibilities and reporting expectations to contracts or service agreements.
Tell staff who work with suppliers what each supplier is and is not responsible for.

requirements.title: Cybersecurity supply chain risk management is integrated into cybersecurity and enterprise risk management, risk assessment, and improvement processes

statement.text: Cybersecurity supply chain risk management is integrated into cybersecurity and enterprise risk management, risk assessment, and improvement processes

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Identify areas of alignment and overlap with cybersecurity and enterprise risk management

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Establish integrated control sets for cybersecurity risk management and cybersecurity supply chain risk management

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Integrate cybersecurity supply chain risk management into improvement processes

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Escalate material cybersecurity risks in supply chains to senior management, and address them at the enterprise risk management level

editorial.question: Is managing supplier and supply chain cybersecurity risk part of your organization's broader risk management, risk assessment, and improvement processes rather than a separate activity?
editorial.whyItMatters: When supplier risk is handled on its own, serious issues with a key vendor may never reach the people weighing the organization's overall risks. Integration means supplier risks are compared, escalated, and improved like any other.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have identified where supply chain risk management overlaps with cybersecurity and enterprise risk management, use an integrated set of controls for both, include supply chain risk in improvement processes, and escalate material supply chain risks to senior management for handling at the enterprise level.
nextSteps: Add significant supplier risks to the same risk register you use for other cybersecurity and business risks.
Use the same rating and review process for supplier risks as for internal risks.
Define when a supplier risk is serious enough to raise with senior management.
Include supplier issues in your regular lessons-learned and improvement reviews.

requirements.title: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality

statement.text: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Develop criteria for supplier criticality based on, for example, the sensitivity of data processed or possessed by suppliers, the degree of access to the organization's systems, and the importance of the products or services to the organization's mission

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Keep a record of all suppliers, and prioritize suppliers based on the criticality criteria

editorial.question: Does your organization keep a record of all its suppliers and rank them by how critical they are to your operations and data?
editorial.whyItMatters: You cannot manage risks from suppliers you do not know about. Ranking them shows where to focus limited time, since a provider holding customer data deserves more scrutiny than an office supply vendor.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You keep a record of all suppliers and have criteria for criticality, such as the sensitivity of data they process or hold, their level of access to your systems, and how important their products or services are to your mission. Each supplier is prioritized against those criteria.
nextSteps: Build a list of all suppliers, starting from accounts payable records and subscriptions.
Define criticality criteria, such as data access, system access, and impact if the supplier failed.
Rate each supplier against the criteria and mark the most critical ones for closer attention.

requirements.title: Requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized, and integrated into contracts and other types of agreements with suppliers and other relevant third parties

statement.text: Requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized, and integrated into contracts and other types of agreements with suppliers and other relevant third parties

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish security requirements for suppliers, products, and services commensurate with their criticality level and potential impact if compromised

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Include all cybersecurity and supply chain requirements that third parties must follow and how compliance with the requirements may be verified in default contractual language

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Define the rules and protocols for information sharing between the organization and its suppliers and sub-tier suppliers in agreements

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Manage risk by including security requirements in agreements based on their criticality and potential impact if compromised

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Define security requirements in service-level agreements (SLAs) for monitoring suppliers for acceptable security performance throughout the supplier relationship lifecycle

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Contractually require suppliers to disclose cybersecurity features, functions, and vulnerabilities of their products and services for the life of the product or the term of service

examples.label: Ex7
examples.text: Contractually require suppliers to provide and maintain a current component inventory (e.g., software or hardware bill of materials) for critical products

examples.label: Ex8
examples.text: Contractually require suppliers to vet their employees and guard against insider threats

examples.label: Ex9
examples.text: Contractually require suppliers to provide evidence of performing acceptable security practices through, for example, self-attestation, conformance to known standards, certifications, or inspections

examples.label: Ex10
examples.text: Specify in contracts and other agreements the rights and responsibilities of the organization, its suppliers, and their supply chains, with respect to potential cybersecurity risks

editorial.question: Do your contracts and agreements with suppliers and other third parties include cybersecurity requirements that match how critical each supplier is?
editorial.whyItMatters: A contract is often your main lever with a supplier. Without written security requirements, you may have no right to be told about a breach at a vendor, ask for evidence of their practices, or require fixes.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have established and prioritized security requirements for suppliers, products, and services based on their criticality and potential impact if compromised, and these are written into contracts and other agreements. Depending on criticality, agreements cover information sharing, how compliance with requirements will be verified, security performance in service-level agreements (formal service commitments), disclosure of vulnerabilities, component inventories for critical products, vetting of supplier staff, evidence of security practices, and each party's rights and responsibilities.
nextSteps: Write standard security clauses for supplier agreements, such as breach notification, data protection, and the right to request evidence of security practices.
Decide which additional requirements apply to your most critical suppliers.
Add the clauses to new contracts, and to existing contracts when they come up for renewal.
Keep a record of which suppliers have agreed to which requirements.

requirements.title: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into formal supplier or other third-party relationships

statement.text: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into formal supplier or other third-party relationships

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Perform thorough due diligence on prospective suppliers that is consistent with procurement planning and commensurate with the level of risk, criticality, and complexity of each supplier relationship

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Assess the suitability of the technology and cybersecurity capabilities and the risk management practices of prospective suppliers

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Conduct supplier risk assessments against business and applicable cybersecurity requirements

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Assess the authenticity, integrity, and security of critical products prior to acquisition and use

editorial.question: Before signing with a new supplier or other third party, does your organization assess their security practices and plan how to reduce the risks they could introduce?
editorial.whyItMatters: It is far simpler to address security concerns before a contract is signed than after. Due diligence helps you avoid suppliers who cannot protect your data or systems and sets expectations from the start.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You plan and perform due diligence on prospective suppliers in proportion to the risk, criticality, and complexity of the relationship. This includes assessing their technology, cybersecurity capabilities, and risk management practices against your business and security requirements, and checking the authenticity, integrity, and security of critical products before you acquire and use them.
nextSteps: Create a short security questionnaire for prospective suppliers, with more depth for critical ones.
Review the answers and any evidence they provide before approving the supplier.
Record the assessment result and any conditions or risk reductions agreed before signing.
For critical products, confirm they come from the genuine source and have not been altered.

requirements.title: The risks posed by a supplier, their products and services, and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

statement.text: The risks posed by a supplier, their products and services, and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Adjust assessment formats and frequencies based on the third party's reputation and the criticality of the products or services they provide

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Evaluate third parties' evidence of compliance with contractual cybersecurity requirements, such as self-attestations, warranties, certifications, and other artifacts

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Monitor critical suppliers to ensure that they are fulfilling their security obligations throughout the supplier relationship lifecycle using a variety of methods and techniques, such as inspections, audits, tests, or other forms of evaluation

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Monitor critical suppliers, services, and products for changes to their risk profiles, and reevaluate supplier criticality and risk impact accordingly

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Plan for unexpected supplier and supply chain-related interruptions to ensure business continuity

editorial.question: Does your organization keep track of the risks each supplier and third party poses, and monitor and respond to them throughout the relationship?
editorial.whyItMatters: A supplier that was safe when you signed can change through a breach, an acquisition, or slipping practices. Ongoing monitoring catches these changes before they become your incident.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Supplier and third-party risks are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored for the life of the relationship. Assessment format and frequency match each supplier's criticality and reputation, evidence of meeting contract requirements is reviewed, critical suppliers are monitored for changes in their risk profile and reassessed, and you have plans for unexpected supplier interruptions.
nextSteps: Set how often each tier of supplier is reassessed, with the most critical reviewed most often.
Request and review updated evidence from critical suppliers, such as security attestations or assessment reports.
Watch for breaches, ownership changes, or service problems at critical suppliers, and reassess when they occur.
Plan how you would keep operating if a critical supplier suddenly became unavailable.

requirements.title: Relevant suppliers and other third parties are included in incident planning, response, and recovery activities

statement.text: Relevant suppliers and other third parties are included in incident planning, response, and recovery activities

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Define and use rules and protocols for reporting incident response and recovery activities and the status between the organization and its suppliers

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify and document the roles and responsibilities of the organization and its suppliers for incident response

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Include critical suppliers in incident response exercises and simulations

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Define and coordinate crisis communication methods and protocols between the organization and its critical suppliers

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Conduct collaborative lessons learned sessions with critical suppliers

editorial.question: Are your relevant suppliers and other third parties included in your incident response planning, exercises, and recovery activities?
editorial.whyItMatters: Many incidents involve a supplier, either as the source or as a partner you need during recovery. Agreeing in advance on who does what and how you will communicate saves critical time during an incident.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have defined how incident response and recovery status is reported between your organization and its suppliers, documented each side's incident response roles, included critical suppliers in exercises and simulations, agreed on crisis communication methods with critical suppliers, and held joint lessons-learned sessions with them.
nextSteps: Add contact details and incident roles for critical suppliers to your incident response plan.
Agree with each critical supplier how and how quickly incidents will be reported in both directions.
Invite critical suppliers to take part in an incident response exercise.
Hold a joint review with the supplier after any incident that involves them.

requirements.title: Supply chain security practices are integrated into cybersecurity and enterprise risk management programs, and their performance is monitored throughout the technology product and service life cycle

statement.text: Supply chain security practices are integrated into cybersecurity and enterprise risk management programs, and their performance is monitored throughout the technology product and service life cycle

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Policies and procedures require provenance records for all acquired technology products and services

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Periodically provide risk reporting to leaders about how acquired components are proven to be untampered and authentic

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Communicate regularly among cybersecurity risk managers and operations personnel about the need to acquire software patches, updates, and upgrades only from authenticated and trustworthy software providers

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Review policies to ensure that they require approved supplier personnel to perform maintenance on supplier products

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Policies and procedure require checking upgrades to critical hardware for unauthorized changes

editorial.question: Does your organization build supply chain security into its risk management and check how well those practices work across the life of the technology you buy?
editorial.whyItMatters: Tampered hardware, counterfeit parts, and malicious software updates can arrive through trusted channels. Confirming where technology comes from and how it is maintained reduces the chance of bringing a compromise in yourself.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Supply chain security practices are part of your cybersecurity and enterprise risk management programs, and their performance is monitored throughout the product and service life cycle. Policies require provenance records (where a product came from) for acquired technology, patches and updates come only from authenticated and trustworthy providers, maintenance is done by approved supplier personnel, upgrades to critical hardware are checked for unauthorized changes, and leaders receive periodic reports on how acquired components are confirmed to be authentic and untampered.
nextSteps: Record the source of each technology purchase, and buy from the manufacturer or authorized sellers.
Configure systems to get software updates only from the vendor's official, verified channels.
Allow only approved supplier personnel to perform maintenance on supplier products.
Report periodically to leadership on how you confirm that acquired technology is authentic and untampered.

requirements.title: Cybersecurity supply chain risk management plans include provisions for activities that occur after the conclusion of a partnership or service agreement

statement.text: Cybersecurity supply chain risk management plans include provisions for activities that occur after the conclusion of a partnership or service agreement

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish processes for terminating critical relationships under both normal and adverse circumstances

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Define and implement plans for component end-of-life maintenance support and obsolescence

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Verify that supplier access to organization resources is deactivated promptly when it is no longer needed

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Verify that assets containing the organization's data are returned or properly disposed of in a timely, controlled, and safe manner

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Develop and execute a plan for terminating or transitioning supplier relationships that takes supply chain security risk and resiliency into account

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Mitigate risks to data and systems created by supplier termination

examples.label: Ex7
examples.text: Manage data leakage risks associated with supplier termination

editorial.question: When a supplier relationship or service agreement ends, does your organization have a plan for removing access, recovering or destroying data, and handling the transition?
editorial.whyItMatters: Ending a relationship carelessly can leave a former vendor with access to your systems, copies of your data, or unsupported products still in use. Planning for the end reduces data leakage and disruption.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Your supply chain risk management plans cover ending relationships under both normal and adverse circumstances. They include promptly deactivating supplier access, returning or safely disposing of assets that contain your data, managing data leakage and other risks created by termination, transitioning suppliers with security and resilience in mind, and planning for end-of-life support and obsolescence of components.
nextSteps: Create a supplier offboarding checklist that covers access removal, data return or destruction, and written confirmation.
Include exit and data return terms in new supplier contracts.
Identify products nearing the end of vendor support and plan their replacement.
For critical suppliers, outline how you would move to an alternative if the relationship ended abruptly.

requirements.title: Inventories of hardware managed by the organization are maintained

statement.text: Inventories of hardware managed by the organization are maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Maintain inventories for all types of hardware, including IT, IoT, OT, and mobile devices

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Constantly monitor networks to detect new hardware and automatically update inventories

editorial.question: Does your organization keep an up-to-date inventory of the hardware it manages, including computers, phones, network equipment, and connected devices?
editorial.whyItMatters: You cannot protect a device you do not know about. Unknown or forgotten devices often miss updates and become an entry point for attackers.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You maintain inventories of all types of hardware you manage, including IT equipment, mobile devices, internet-connected devices such as cameras and smart equipment, and operational technology (equipment that controls physical processes) if you have it. Where practical, network monitoring detects new hardware and updates the inventory automatically.
nextSteps: List every device you own or manage, with its type, user or owner, and location.
Include phones, printers, routers, cameras, and other connected devices, not only computers.
Assign someone to update the list when devices are bought, reassigned, or retired.
Consider a tool that detects new devices on your network and flags them for review.

requirements.title: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained

statement.text: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Maintain inventories for all types of software and services, including commercial-off-the-shelf, open-source, custom applications, API services, and cloud-based applications and services

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Constantly monitor all platforms, including containers and virtual machines, for software and service inventory changes

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Maintain an inventory of the organization's systems

editorial.question: Does your organization keep an up-to-date inventory of the software, online services, and systems it manages, including cloud applications?
editorial.whyItMatters: Software you do not know about cannot be updated, licensed, or secured. An inventory also lets you respond quickly when a vulnerability is announced in a product you might be using.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You maintain inventories of all types of software and services, including commercial, open-source, and custom-built applications, application programming interface (API) services, and cloud-based applications, as well as an inventory of your systems. Where practical, platforms such as virtual machines and containers are monitored for software and service changes.
nextSteps: List the software installed on your devices and the cloud services your staff use, with an owner for each.
Record the systems your organization runs and the software each one includes.
Review the list at a frequency you define and whenever new software or services are adopted.
Use device management or inventory tools to detect software changes automatically where possible.

requirements.title: Representations of the organization's authorized network communication and internal and external network data flows are maintained

statement.text: Representations of the organization's authorized network communication and internal and external network data flows are maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Maintain baselines of communication and data flows within the organization's wired and wireless networks

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Maintain baselines of communication and data flows between the organization and third parties

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Maintain baselines of communication and data flows for the organization's infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) usage

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Maintain documentation of expected network ports, protocols, and services that are typically used among authorized systems

editorial.question: Does your organization maintain an up-to-date picture of how data is expected to flow across its networks and to and from outside parties?
editorial.whyItMatters: Knowing what normal network traffic looks like makes it possible to spot unusual connections and to protect the paths sensitive data takes. It also shows where data leaves your control.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You maintain documentation, such as network diagrams and data flow maps, of authorized communication and data flows within your wired and wireless networks, between your organization and third parties, and within any cloud infrastructure you use. The network ports, protocols, and services expected between authorized systems are documented.
nextSteps: Draw a basic diagram of your network showing key systems, internet connections, and wireless networks.
Map where sensitive data travels, including to cloud services and partners.
Document which network ports and services your systems are expected to use.
Update the diagrams when you add systems, services, or connections.

requirements.title: Inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained

statement.text: Inventories of services provided by suppliers are maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Inventory all external services used by the organization, including third-party infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS), platform-as-a-service (PaaS), and software-as-a-service (SaaS) offerings; APIs; and other externally hosted application services

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Update the inventory when a new external service is going to be utilized to ensure adequate cybersecurity risk management monitoring of the organization's use of that service

editorial.question: Does your organization keep an up-to-date list of the services it receives from suppliers, such as cloud applications, hosting, and externally hosted tools?
editorial.whyItMatters: Outside services often hold sensitive data and connect to your systems, yet staff can sign up for them without anyone keeping track. A current list makes sure each one is included in your security oversight.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You maintain an inventory of all external services you use, including cloud infrastructure, platform, and software services, application programming interfaces (APIs), and other externally hosted applications. The inventory is updated before a new external service is put into use so it can be included in risk management and monitoring.
nextSteps: List every external service your organization uses, including free tools, with the business owner and the data each holds.
Check billing and expense records for subscriptions that are not on the list.
Require that new services be added to the list, and reviewed for security, before they are used.

requirements.title: Assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission

statement.text: Assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Define criteria for prioritizing each class of assets

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Apply the prioritization criteria to assets

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Track the asset priorities and update them periodically or when significant changes to the organization occur

editorial.question: Has your organization ranked its assets, such as systems, data, and devices, by how sensitive and critical they are and how much their loss would affect the mission?
editorial.whyItMatters: Not every asset needs the same protection. Prioritizing shows where to spend limited time and money first, and which systems to restore first after an incident.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have defined criteria for prioritizing each class of asset based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission, and applied them to your assets. You track the resulting priorities and update them periodically and when significant changes occur.
nextSteps: Define a few priority levels and the criteria for each, such as data sensitivity and the effect on operations if the asset were lost.
