Assign a priority to each item in your hardware, software, service, and data inventories.
Review priorities at an interval you define and after major changes, such as a new line of business or an acquisition.

requirements.title: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained

statement.text: Inventories of data and corresponding metadata for designated data types are maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Maintain a list of the designated data types of interest (e.g., personally identifiable information, protected health information, financial account numbers, organization intellectual property, operational technology data)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Continuously discover and analyze ad hoc data to identify new instances of designated data types

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Assign data classifications to designated data types through tags or labels

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Track the provenance, data owner, and geolocation of each instance of designated data types

editorial.question: Does your organization keep an inventory of where its important types of data, such as personal, financial, or health information, are stored and who owns them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Sensitive data spreads into email, shared drives, and cloud services over time. Knowing where it lives is necessary to protect it, respond to a breach, and meet privacy obligations.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have a list of designated data types of interest, such as personal information, health information, financial account numbers, and intellectual property, and an inventory of where instances of that data reside. Data is tagged or labeled with a classification, its source, owner, and geographic location are tracked, and discovery is used to find new instances where practical.
nextSteps: Decide which types of data you need to track, such as customer personal information or payment details.
List the systems, services, and locations where each type is stored, and name an owner for each.
Label the data, or the systems that hold it, with a classification.
Search shared drives and cloud storage periodically for sensitive data in unexpected places.

requirements.title: Systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles

statement.text: Systems, hardware, software, services, and data are managed throughout their life cycles

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Integrate cybersecurity considerations throughout the life cycles of systems, hardware, software, and services

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Integrate cybersecurity considerations into product life cycles

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Identify unofficial uses of technology to meet mission objectives (i.e., shadow IT)

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Periodically identify redundant systems, hardware, software, and services that unnecessarily increase the organization's attack surface

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Properly configure and secure systems, hardware, software, and services prior to their deployment in production

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Update inventories when systems, hardware, software, and services are moved or transferred within the organization

examples.label: Ex7
examples.text: Securely destroy stored data based on the organization's data retention policy using the prescribed destruction method, and keep and manage a record of the destructions

examples.label: Ex8
examples.text: Securely sanitize data storage when hardware is being retired, decommissioned, reassigned, or sent for repairs or replacement

examples.label: Ex9
examples.text: Offer methods for destroying paper, storage media, and other physical forms of data storage

editorial.question: Does your organization manage security for its systems, hardware, software, services, and data across their whole life, from acquisition and setup to retirement and disposal?
editorial.whyItMatters: Risks appear at every stage: insecure default settings at setup, forgotten systems that stop receiving updates, and old drives discarded with data still on them. Managing the full life cycle closes these gaps.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Security is considered throughout the life cycles of your systems, hardware, software, services, and data. Assets are configured securely before use, inventories are updated when assets move, unofficial technology (shadow IT) and redundant assets are identified, data is destroyed according to your retention policy with records kept, storage is sanitized before hardware is retired, reassigned, or sent for repair, and methods are available for destroying paper and other physical media.
nextSteps: Create a setup checklist that secures new devices and services before they go into use.
Review your inventories periodically for unused, redundant, or unapproved technology, and remove or approve it.
Wipe or destroy storage before any device is retired, reassigned, or sent for repair, and keep a record.
Provide a secure way to dispose of paper records and removable media, such as a shredder or a disposal service.

requirements.title: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded

statement.text: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use vulnerability management technologies to identify unpatched and misconfigured software

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Assess network and system architectures for design and implementation weaknesses that affect cybersecurity

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Review, analyze, or test organization-developed software to identify design, coding, and default configuration vulnerabilities

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Assess facilities that house critical computing assets for physical vulnerabilities and resilience issues

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Monitor sources of cyber threat intelligence for information on new vulnerabilities in products and services

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Review processes and procedures for weaknesses that could be exploited to affect cybersecurity

editorial.question: Does your organization regularly look for weaknesses in its systems, software, facilities, and processes, confirm which ones are real, and record them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Unpatched software and misconfigured systems are among the most common ways attackers get in. Finding and recording weaknesses is the first step to fixing them before someone else exploits them.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You identify, validate, and record vulnerabilities (weaknesses that could be exploited) in your assets. This includes using tools to find unpatched and misconfigured software, assessing network and system design, reviewing or testing software you develop, assessing facilities that house critical systems, monitoring threat intelligence for newly announced vulnerabilities, and reviewing processes for exploitable weaknesses.
nextSteps: Run a vulnerability scanning tool across your devices and systems at a frequency you define.
Sign up for security notices from the vendors of your key software and devices.
Record each confirmed vulnerability with the affected asset, its severity, and an owner.
Review locations that house critical equipment, and processes such as payment approvals, for weaknesses that could be exploited.

requirements.title: Cyber threat intelligence is received from information sharing forums and sources

statement.text: Cyber threat intelligence is received from information sharing forums and sources

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Configure cybersecurity tools and technologies with detection or response capabilities to securely ingest cyber threat intelligence feeds

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Receive and review advisories from reputable third parties on current threat actors and their tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs)

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Monitor sources of cyber threat intelligence for information on the types of vulnerabilities that emerging technologies may have

editorial.question: Does your organization receive and review cyber threat information from trusted sources, such as government advisories, industry groups, or security providers?
editorial.whyItMatters: Threat information tells you what attackers are doing now and which weaknesses they are targeting. Without it, you may learn about a relevant threat only after it reaches you.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You receive cyber threat intelligence (information about current threats, attackers, and their methods) from information sharing forums and reputable sources, and someone reviews advisories about threat actors and their tactics. Security tools with detection or response features are configured to securely take in threat intelligence feeds, and you watch for the kinds of vulnerabilities that emerging technologies may have.
nextSteps: Subscribe to free cybersecurity alerts from your national cybersecurity agency.
Join an information sharing group for your industry or region, if one exists.
Assign someone to review alerts on a regular schedule and pass on anything that affects your systems.
Turn on threat intelligence features in your existing security tools where they are available.

requirements.title: Internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded

statement.text: Internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use cyber threat intelligence to maintain awareness of the types of threat actors likely to target the organization and the TTPs they are likely to use

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Perform threat hunting to look for signs of threat actors within the environment

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Implement processes for identifying internal threat actors

editorial.question: Has your organization identified and recorded the internal and external threats it faces, such as criminal groups, fraudsters, or insiders, and how they might attack?
editorial.whyItMatters: Different organizations attract different attackers. Knowing who is likely to target you, and how, helps you focus defenses on the methods that matter most for your situation.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You keep a record of the internal and external threats relevant to you, using threat intelligence to understand the kinds of threat actors likely to target you and the tactics, techniques, and procedures (methods) they tend to use. You have processes for identifying internal threat actors and, where you have the capability, actively look for signs of attackers already in your environment (threat hunting).
nextSteps: List the kinds of attackers likely to target an organization like yours, such as ransomware groups, payment fraudsters, or insiders.
Note the methods each tends to use, drawing on the threat alerts you receive.
Set up a way to identify insider threats, such as reviewing unusual access by staff.
Update the threat list when you see new advisories or experience an incident.

requirements.title: Potential impacts and likelihoods of threats exploiting vulnerabilities are identified and recorded

statement.text: Potential impacts and likelihoods of threats exploiting vulnerabilities are identified and recorded

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Business leaders and cybersecurity risk management practitioners work together to estimate the likelihood and impact of risk scenarios and record them in risk registers

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Enumerate the potential business impacts of unauthorized access to the organization's communications, systems, and data processed in or by those systems

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Account for the potential impacts of cascading failures for systems of systems

editorial.question: Has your organization estimated and recorded how likely it is that threats will exploit its weaknesses and what the business impact would be?
editorial.whyItMatters: Likelihood and impact turn a long list of weaknesses into a clear picture of what could actually hurt the business. That picture lets you decide what to address first.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Business leaders and the people managing cybersecurity risk work together to estimate the likelihood and impact of risk scenarios and record them, often in a risk register. You have listed the potential business impacts of unauthorized access to your communications, systems, and data, and you account for cascading failures, where one system's failure affects others.
nextSteps: Write a handful of realistic risk scenarios, such as ransomware on your main file server or a stolen laptop holding customer data.
With business leaders, estimate how likely each scenario is and what it would cost in money, downtime, and reputation.
Record the estimates in your risk register.
Note where one failure could trigger others, such as an email outage stopping order processing.

requirements.title: Threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts are used to understand inherent risk and inform risk response prioritization

statement.text: Threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts are used to understand inherent risk and inform risk response prioritization

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Develop threat models to better understand risks to the data and identify appropriate risk responses

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Prioritize cybersecurity resource allocations and investments based on estimated likelihoods and impacts

editorial.question: Does your organization combine what it knows about threats, weaknesses, likelihood, and impact to understand its overall risk and decide which risks to address first?
editorial.whyItMatters: Combining these factors keeps attention and money on the risks that matter most, rather than on whatever seems most alarming. It also gives you a defensible basis for prioritizing security work.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts are used together to understand inherent risk (risk before additional safeguards) and to prioritize risk responses. Threat models help you understand risks to your data, and cybersecurity resources and investments are prioritized based on estimated likelihood and impact.
nextSteps: For each risk in your register, combine its likelihood and impact into an overall rating using your agreed method.
Rank the risks and use the ranking to decide where to spend time and budget.
For your most sensitive data or systems, walk through how an attacker might reach them to identify the protections you need.

requirements.title: Risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked, and communicated

statement.text: Risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked, and communicated

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Apply the vulnerability management plan's criteria for deciding whether to accept, transfer, mitigate, or avoid risk

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Apply the vulnerability management plan's criteria for selecting compensating controls to mitigate risk

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Track the progress of risk response implementation (e.g., plan of action and milestones (POA&M), risk register, risk detail report)

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Use risk assessment findings to inform risk response decisions and actions

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Communicate planned risk responses to affected stakeholders in priority order

editorial.question: When your organization identifies a cybersecurity risk, does it choose a response, plan it, track progress, and tell the people affected?
editorial.whyItMatters: Identifying risks has little value if nothing is done about them. Tracked, communicated responses make sure decisions are carried out and that people know what changes are coming.
editorial.doneLooksLike: For each risk, you choose whether to accept, transfer, reduce, or avoid it using defined criteria, including criteria for selecting compensating controls (alternative safeguards). Responses are prioritized and planned based on risk assessment findings, progress is tracked, for example in a risk register or a plan of action with milestones, and planned responses are communicated to affected stakeholders in priority order.
nextSteps: For each high-priority risk, decide whether to accept, transfer, reduce, or avoid it, and record the reason.
Assign an owner and target date to each planned response.
Review progress at regular meetings and update the risk register.
Tell the people affected about planned changes, starting with the highest-priority ones.

requirements.title: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked

statement.text: Changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded, and tracked

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Implement and follow procedures for the formal documentation, review, testing, and approval of proposed changes and requested exceptions

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Document the possible risks of making or not making each proposed change, and provide guidance on rolling back changes

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Document the risks related to each requested exception and the plan for responding to those risks

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Periodically review risks that were accepted based upon planned future actions or milestones

editorial.question: Does your organization assess and record the risk of changes to its systems, and of exceptions to its security rules, before approving them, and then track them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Unreviewed changes are a common cause of outages and new security gaps, and exceptions that are never revisited can quietly become permanent. Managing both keeps risk visible and under control.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Proposed changes and requested exceptions are formally documented, reviewed, tested, and approved. For each change you record the risks of making it and of not making it and how to roll it back, for each exception you record the related risks and the plan for responding to them, and you periodically review risks that were accepted on the basis of planned future actions.
nextSteps: Set up a request form or ticket for system changes that records the reason, risk, test plan, and rollback steps.
Require approval from a named person before significant changes go ahead.
Keep a list of approved exceptions to security rules, each with an owner, the risk, and a review or end date.
Review the exception list periodically and close or renew each entry.

requirements.title: Processes for receiving, analyzing, and responding to vulnerability disclosures are established

statement.text: Processes for receiving, analyzing, and responding to vulnerability disclosures are established

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Conduct vulnerability information sharing between the organization and its suppliers following the rules and protocols defined in contracts

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Assign responsibilities and verify the execution of procedures for processing, analyzing the impact of, and responding to cybersecurity threat, vulnerability, or incident disclosures by suppliers, customers, partners, and government cybersecurity organizations

editorial.question: Does your organization have a process for receiving, analyzing, and responding to reports of security weaknesses from suppliers, customers, partners, or government agencies?
editorial.whyItMatters: Others may find problems in your systems, or in products you use, before you do. A clear process makes sure these reports reach the right person and lead to timely action instead of being lost.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Responsibilities are assigned, and their execution verified, for receiving, analyzing the impact of, and responding to threat, vulnerability, or incident disclosures from suppliers, customers, partners, and government cybersecurity organizations. Vulnerability information is exchanged with suppliers according to the rules and protocols in your contracts.
nextSteps: Assign a person or role to receive and assess vulnerability reports.
Publish a way for outsiders to report security issues to you, such as a dedicated email address.
Define steps for confirming a report, assessing its impact, responding, and informing the reporter.
Follow the information sharing terms in supplier contracts when exchanging vulnerability information.

requirements.title: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use

statement.text: The authenticity and integrity of hardware and software are assessed prior to acquisition and use

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Assess the authenticity and cybersecurity of critical technology products and services prior to acquisition and use

editorial.question: Before buying or installing hardware and software, does your organization check that it is genuine and has not been tampered with?
editorial.whyItMatters: Counterfeit devices and altered software can carry hidden malicious code or fail unexpectedly. Checking authenticity and integrity before use keeps compromised products out of your environment.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You assess the authenticity and integrity of hardware and software before acquiring and using them, with particular attention to the authenticity and cybersecurity of critical technology products and services.
nextSteps: Buy hardware and software only from the manufacturer or its authorized resellers.
Download software only from official sources, and verify digital signatures or checksums (codes that confirm a file is unaltered) where they are provided.
Inspect critical hardware on arrival for signs of tampering or counterfeiting.

requirements.title: Critical suppliers are assessed prior to acquisition

statement.text: Critical suppliers are assessed prior to acquisition

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Conduct supplier risk assessments against business and applicable cybersecurity requirements, including the supply chain

editorial.question: Before acquiring products or services from a supplier you will depend on heavily, does your organization assess the security risks that supplier brings?
editorial.whyItMatters: Critical suppliers can have deep access to your data or operations, so their weaknesses can become yours. Assessing them before you commit gives you the chance to negotiate safeguards or choose another provider.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Critical suppliers are assessed before acquisition against your business and cybersecurity requirements, including the risks in their own supply chains, and the results inform the decision to proceed.
nextSteps: Use your supplier criticality criteria to decide which prospective suppliers need a full assessment.
Assess each critical supplier against your business and security requirements before signing, including how they manage their own suppliers.
Document the result and any conditions for approval, and keep it with the contract file.

requirements.title: Improvements are identified from evaluations

statement.text: Improvements are identified from evaluations

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Perform self-assessments of critical services that take current threats and TTPs into consideration

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Invest in third-party assessments or independent audits of the effectiveness of the organization's cybersecurity program to identify areas that need improvement

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Constantly evaluate compliance with selected cybersecurity requirements through automated means

editorial.question: Does your organization use self-assessments, independent audits, or other evaluations of its cybersecurity program to identify specific improvements?
editorial.whyItMatters: Evaluations show where practice falls short of intent. Turning their findings into a list of improvements keeps the program moving forward instead of repeating the same gaps.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You identify improvements from evaluations, such as self-assessments of critical services that take current threats and attacker methods into account, third-party assessments or independent audits of your program's effectiveness, and automated checks against the cybersecurity requirements you have selected.
nextSteps: Complete a self-assessment of your cybersecurity program, such as this one, at a frequency you define.
Consider an independent assessment of your most critical services.
Record each finding as an improvement item with an owner and a priority.

requirements.title: Improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties

statement.text: Improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Identify improvements for future incident response activities based on findings from incident response assessments (e.g., tabletop exercises and simulations, tests, internal reviews, independent audits)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Identify improvements for future business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response activities based on exercises performed in coordination with critical service providers and product suppliers

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Involve internal stakeholders (e.g., senior executives, legal department, HR) in security tests and exercises as appropriate

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Perform penetration testing to identify opportunities to improve the security posture of selected high-risk systems as approved by leadership

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Exercise contingency plans for responding to and recovering from the discovery that products or services did not originate with the contracted supplier or partner or were altered before receipt

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Collect and analyze performance metrics using security tools and services to inform improvements to the cybersecurity program

editorial.question: Does your organization run security tests and exercises, including some with key suppliers, and use the results to identify improvements?
editorial.whyItMatters: Tests and exercises show how plans and defenses perform under realistic conditions before a real incident does. Including suppliers reveals gaps at the handoffs between organizations.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You identify improvements from tests and exercises, such as tabletop exercises (guided discussions of a scenario), simulations, internal reviews, independent audits, and leadership-approved penetration tests (authorized simulated attacks) of selected high-risk systems. Some business continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response exercises involve critical service providers and suppliers, including scenarios where products turn out to be counterfeit or altered, internal stakeholders such as executives, legal, and HR take part as appropriate, and performance metrics from security tools also inform improvements.
nextSteps: Run a tabletop exercise on a realistic scenario, such as ransomware, with leadership and key staff.
Invite a critical supplier or service provider to join an exercise that depends on them.
Consider a penetration test of your highest-risk systems, with leadership approval.
Record the improvements identified and assign an owner to each.

requirements.title: Improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities

statement.text: Improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures, and activities

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Conduct collaborative lessons learned sessions with suppliers

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Annually review cybersecurity policies, processes, and procedures to take lessons learned into account

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Use metrics to assess operational cybersecurity performance over time

editorial.question: Does your organization review how its everyday security processes and procedures work in practice and use those lessons to identify improvements?
editorial.whyItMatters: Running a process reveals problems that plans miss, such as steps that are skipped or take too long. Capturing those lessons makes the next run better.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Improvements are identified from carrying out operational processes, procedures, and activities. You hold lessons-learned sessions, including with suppliers, review policies, processes, and procedures periodically (for example annually) to take lessons learned into account, and use metrics to assess operational security performance over time.
nextSteps: After significant operational work, such as a system migration or an access review, note what worked and what did not.
Hold lessons-learned sessions with suppliers whose services affect your security.
Review your security policies and procedures on a schedule you define, for example once a year, to incorporate lessons learned.
Track a few operational measures over time, such as time to apply updates, to spot trends.

requirements.title: Incident response plans and other cybersecurity plans that affect operations are established, communicated, maintained, and improved

statement.text: Incident response plans and other cybersecurity plans that affect operations are established, communicated, maintained, and improved

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish contingency plans (e.g., incident response, business continuity, disaster recovery) for responding to and recovering from adverse events that can interfere with operations, expose confidential information, or otherwise endanger the organization's mission and viability

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Include contact and communication information, processes for handling common scenarios, and criteria for prioritization, escalation, and elevation in all contingency plans

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Create a vulnerability management plan to identify and assess all types of vulnerabilities and to prioritize, test, and implement risk responses

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Communicate cybersecurity plans (including updates) to those responsible for carrying them out and to affected parties

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Review and update all cybersecurity plans annually or when a need for significant improvements is identified

editorial.question: Does your organization have incident response and other operational cybersecurity plans that are written, shared with the people who carry them out, and kept up to date?
editorial.whyItMatters: During an incident there is little time to work out who does what. Current plans that the right people know about help limit damage, restore operations sooner, and protect the organization's reputation.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have contingency plans, such as incident response, business continuity, and disaster recovery plans, and a vulnerability management plan. The contingency plans include contact and communication details, procedures for common scenarios, and criteria for prioritization and escalation, and all plans and their updates are communicated to those responsible and to affected parties, then reviewed and improved periodically (for example annually) and when significant improvements are needed.
nextSteps: Write or update an incident response plan with contact details, roles, steps for common scenarios, and escalation criteria.
Create business continuity and disaster recovery plans for your critical services, and a plan for managing vulnerabilities.
Share each plan, and each update, with everyone who has a role in it.
Set a review date for each plan, and update it after exercises, incidents, or major changes.

requirements.title: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization

statement.text: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed by the organization

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Initiate requests for new access or additional access for employees, contractors, and others, and track, review, and fulfill the requests, with permission from system or data owners when needed

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Issue, manage, and revoke cryptographic certificates and identity tokens, cryptographic keys (i.e., key management), and other credentials

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Select a unique identifier for each device from immutable hardware characteristics or an identifier securely provisioned to the device

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Physically label authorized hardware with an identifier for inventory and servicing purposes

editorial.question: Does your organization manage the accounts, passwords, keys, and other credentials used by its people, services, and devices, from issuing them to revoking them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Every account, service login, and device identity is a possible way in. If nobody tracks who and what holds credentials, old or unneeded ones linger and can be misused without anyone noticing.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Requests for new or additional access are tracked, reviewed, and fulfilled, with approval from system or data owners when needed. Certificates, identity tokens, cryptographic keys, and other credentials are issued, managed, and revoked deliberately, and each authorized device has a unique identifier, with hardware physically labeled for inventory and servicing.
nextSteps: Set up one way to request, approve, and record new or changed access, with the system or data owner approving when needed.
List the credentials your organization depends on, including service accounts, certificates, and cryptographic keys, and note who manages and revokes each.
Give each authorized device a unique identifier and label hardware so it can be matched to your inventory.
Revoke credentials promptly when people leave, services are retired, or devices are disposed of.

requirements.title: Identities are proofed and bound to credentials based on the context of interactions

statement.text: Identities are proofed and bound to credentials based on the context of interactions

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Verify a person's claimed identity at enrollment time using government-issued identity credentials (e.g., passport, visa, driver's license)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Issue a different credential for each person (i.e., no credential sharing)

editorial.question: Before issuing an account or credential, does your organization confirm that the person is who they claim to be, with checks that fit what the access allows?
editorial.whyItMatters: If someone can obtain an account by claiming to be someone else, every other access control rests on a false identity. Shared credentials cause a similar problem: you can no longer tell who did what.
editorial.doneLooksLike: At enrollment, you verify each person's claimed identity (identity proofing) with checks suited to the context, such as government-issued identification for higher-risk access, and bind the verified identity to their credential. Each person receives their own credential, and credentials are not shared.
nextSteps: Decide which identity checks are needed before granting each kind of access, with stronger checks for more sensitive access.
Verify identity in person or through a trusted process before issuing credentials to new staff, contractors, and others.
Replace shared logins with individual accounts so every action can be traced to one person.

requirements.title: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated

statement.text: Users, services, and hardware are authenticated

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Require multifactor authentication

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Enforce policies for the minimum strength of passwords, PINs, and similar authenticators

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Periodically reauthenticate users, services, and hardware based on risk (e.g., in zero trust architectures)

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Ensure that authorized personnel can access accounts essential for protecting safety under emergency conditions

editorial.question: Does your organization require people, services, and devices to prove their identity before gaining access, for example with multi-factor authentication for user logins?
editorial.whyItMatters: Stolen and guessed passwords are among the most common ways attackers get in. Strong authentication makes a stolen password far less useful on its own.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Multi-factor authentication (a second check beyond a password) is required, and minimum strength rules apply to passwords, PINs, and similar authenticators. Users, services, and devices are reauthenticated periodically based on risk, and authorized personnel can still reach accounts essential to protecting safety in an emergency.
nextSteps: Turn on multi-factor authentication, starting with email, remote access, administrator accounts, and cloud services.
Set minimum strength rules for passwords and PINs, and give staff a password manager to help meet them.
Decide how often sessions and device connections must reauthenticate, based on the risk of what they reach.
Document how authorized people can reach accounts essential to safety during an emergency.

requirements.title: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified

statement.text: Identity assertions are protected, conveyed, and verified

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Protect identity assertions that are used to convey authentication and user information through single sign-on systems

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Protect identity assertions that are used to convey authentication and user information between federated systems

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Implement standards-based approaches for identity assertions in all contexts, and follow all guidance for the generation (e.g., data models, metadata), protection (e.g., digital signing, encryption), and verification (e.g., signature validation) of identity assertions

editorial.question: When your organization uses single sign-on or lets one system vouch for a user to another, are those identity assertions protected in transit and verified on receipt?
editorial.whyItMatters: Single sign-on (one login that grants access to many services) works by passing a signed statement, called an identity assertion, about who the user is. If that statement can be forged, intercepted, or replayed, an attacker can get in without ever knowing a password.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Identity assertions passed through single sign-on and between federated systems (separate organizations or services that trust each other's logins) use standards-based approaches. They are generated, digitally signed or encrypted, and verified according to the applicable guidance, and receiving systems validate signatures before accepting them.
nextSteps: List the services that rely on single sign-on or accept logins from another identity provider.
Confirm that each integration uses a standards-based protocol with signing, and encryption where supported, turned on.
Check that every receiving service validates assertion signatures and rejects assertions that fail validation.
Follow your identity provider's configuration guidance and revisit integrations when that guidance changes.

requirements.title: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

statement.text: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined in a policy, managed, enforced, and reviewed, and incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Review logical and physical access privileges periodically and whenever someone changes roles or leaves the organization, and promptly rescind privileges that are no longer needed

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Take attributes of the requester and the requested resource into account for authorization decisions (e.g., geolocation, day/time, requester endpoint's cyber health)

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Restrict access and privileges to the minimum necessary (e.g., zero trust architecture)

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Periodically review the privileges associated with critical business functions to confirm proper separation of duties

editorial.question: Does your organization give people only the access their role needs, follow a written access policy, and review permissions regularly and when roles change?
editorial.whyItMatters: Broad access turns one compromised account into a much larger problem. Splitting sensitive tasks between people also makes fraud and errors harder to carry out unnoticed.
editorial.doneLooksLike: A policy defines how access permissions and authorizations are granted, and they are managed and enforced according to it. Access is limited to the minimum needed (least privilege), and critical business functions are split so no single person controls them end to end (separation of duties). Logical and physical access is reviewed periodically and when people change roles or leave, and privileges that are no longer needed are removed promptly.
nextSteps: Write down who approves access to each key system and what each role should be able to do.
Remove administrator rights and other privileges people do not need for their current work.
Review access periodically and whenever someone changes roles or leaves, and rescind what is no longer needed.
Split critical tasks, such as approving and sending payments, between different people.

requirements.title: Physical access to assets is managed, monitored, and enforced commensurate with risk

statement.text: Physical access to assets is managed, monitored, and enforced commensurate with risk

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use security guards, security cameras, locked entrances, alarm systems, and other physical controls to monitor facilities and restrict access

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Employ additional physical security controls for areas that contain high-risk assets

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Escort guests, vendors, and other third parties within areas that contain business-critical assets

editorial.question: Does your organization control and monitor who can physically reach its offices, equipment, and records, with stronger protection where the risk is higher?
editorial.whyItMatters: Someone who can walk up to a server, network closet, or unattended laptop can often bypass technical safeguards. Physical controls limit that kind of access to the people who need it.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Physical controls such as locked entrances, alarm systems, cameras, or guards restrict and monitor access to your facilities in proportion to risk. Areas holding high-risk assets have additional protection, and guests, vendors, and other third parties are escorted in areas with business-critical assets.
nextSteps: Identify the rooms and equipment that hold your most important assets, such as servers, network equipment, and paper records.
Lock those areas and limit keys or badges to the people who need them.
Escort visitors and vendors whenever they are in sensitive areas.
Add monitoring, such as an alarm or camera, where the risk justifies it.

requirements.title: Personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind

statement.text: Personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Provide basic cybersecurity awareness and training to employees, contractors, partners, suppliers, and all other users of the organization's non-public resources

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Train personnel to recognize social engineering attempts and other common attacks, report attacks and suspicious activity, comply with acceptable use policies, and perform basic cyber hygiene tasks (e.g., patching software, choosing passwords, protecting credentials)

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Explain the consequences of cybersecurity policy violations, both to individual users and the organization as a whole

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Periodically assess or test users on their understanding of basic cybersecurity practices

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Require annual refreshers to reinforce existing practices and introduce new practices

editorial.question: Do your staff, contractors, and other users receive cybersecurity awareness training that helps them spot common attacks and handle everyday tasks safely?
editorial.whyItMatters: Many attacks begin with a convincing email, call, or message aimed at an ordinary employee. People who know what to look for, and how to report it, catch problems that technology misses.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Everyone who uses your non-public resources, including contractors, partners, and suppliers, receives basic training on recognizing social engineering (manipulating people into revealing information or taking harmful actions), reporting suspicious activity, following acceptable use policies, and basic hygiene such as updating software, choosing passwords, and protecting credentials. Training explains the consequences of policy violations, understanding is assessed periodically, and refreshers are given on a regular schedule, such as annually.
nextSteps: Choose or create a short awareness course covering phishing, passwords, credential protection, software updates, and how to report concerns.
Make the training part of onboarding for employees and for contractors and others who use your systems.
Check understanding periodically, for example with quizzes or simulated phishing messages.
Schedule refreshers and update the content as attack methods change.

requirements.title: Individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind

statement.text: Individuals in specialized roles are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Identify the specialized roles within the organization that require additional cybersecurity training, such as physical and cybersecurity personnel, finance personnel, senior leadership, and anyone with access to business-critical data

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Provide role-based cybersecurity awareness and training to all those in specialized roles, including contractors, partners, suppliers, and other third parties

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Periodically assess or test users on their understanding of cybersecurity practices for their specialized roles

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Require annual refreshers to reinforce existing practices and introduce new practices

editorial.question: Do people in roles with greater cybersecurity exposure, such as finance, leadership, IT, and security staff, receive additional training specific to their duties?
editorial.whyItMatters: Some roles are targeted more often or can do more damage if deceived. A person who approves payments or an administrator with broad access needs knowledge beyond general awareness.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You have identified the roles that need more training, such as physical and cybersecurity staff, finance personnel, senior leadership, and anyone with access to business-critical data. People in those roles, including contractors, partners, suppliers, and other third parties, receive role-based training, their understanding is assessed periodically, and refreshers are given on a regular schedule.
nextSteps: List the roles in your organization that handle money, business-critical data, administrator access, or security duties.
Provide training tailored to each role, such as payment fraud for finance or secure administration for IT.
Include contractors and other third parties who fill those roles.
Assess understanding periodically and refresh the training on a set schedule.

requirements.title: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected

statement.text: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use encryption, digital signatures, and cryptographic hashes to protect the confidentiality and integrity of stored data in files, databases, virtual machine disk images, container images, and other resources

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Use full disk encryption to protect data stored on user endpoints

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Confirm the integrity of software by validating signatures

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Restrict the use of removable media to prevent data exfiltration

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Physically secure removable media containing unencrypted sensitive information, such as within locked offices or file cabinets

editorial.question: Does your organization protect stored data, on laptops, servers, cloud storage, and removable media, from unauthorized viewing, alteration, or loss?
editorial.whyItMatters: A lost laptop, stolen drive, or breached file store exposes whatever is on it unless the data is protected. Encryption and integrity checks help keep stored information private and trustworthy.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Stored data in files, databases, and virtual machine or container images is protected with encryption, and with digital signatures or cryptographic hashes where integrity matters. Laptops and other endpoints use full disk encryption, software signatures are validated, removable media use is restricted, and removable media holding unencrypted sensitive information is physically secured.
nextSteps: Turn on full disk encryption for all laptops, desktops, and mobile devices.
Confirm that databases, file shares, and cloud storage holding sensitive data are encrypted.
Restrict the use of USB drives and other removable media, and lock up any that hold unencrypted sensitive information.

requirements.title: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-transit are protected

statement.text: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-transit are protected

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use encryption, digital signatures, and cryptographic hashes to protect the confidentiality and integrity of network communications

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Automatically encrypt or block outbound emails and other communications that contain sensitive data, depending on the data classification

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Block access to personal email, file sharing, file storage services, and other personal communications applications and services from organizational systems and networks

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Prevent reuse of sensitive data from production environments (e.g., customer records) in development, testing, and other non-production environments

editorial.question: Does your organization protect data as it travels across networks, including email and web traffic, so it cannot be read or altered along the way?
editorial.whyItMatters: Data moving over the internet or a shared network can be intercepted or tampered with. Data can also leave through personal email or file-sharing accounts that your organization does not control.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Network communications are encrypted, with digital signatures or hashes protecting integrity where needed. Depending on your risk and how data is classified, outgoing email and other messages containing sensitive data are automatically encrypted or blocked, personal email and file-sharing services are blocked from organizational systems, and production data such as customer records is kept out of development and test environments.
nextSteps: Require encrypted connections for your websites, remote access, and email.
Set rules that encrypt or block outgoing messages containing sensitive data.
Decide whether to block personal email and file-sharing services on work devices and networks.
Use made-up or masked data, rather than real customer records, for development and testing.

requirements.title: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-use are protected

statement.text: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-in-use are protected

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Remove data that must remain confidential (e.g., from processors and memory) as soon as it is no longer needed

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Protect data in use from access by other users and processes of the same platform

editorial.question: Does your organization protect sensitive data while applications are actively using it, so other users and processes on the same system cannot reach it?
editorial.whyItMatters: Data usually has to be decrypted while it is being worked on, which makes memory a target. An attacker with a foothold on a shared system may try to read data belonging to other programs or users.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Data that must stay confidential is removed from memory and processors as soon as it is no longer needed. Systems keep data in use isolated from other users and processes running on the same platform.
nextSteps: Identify the systems that process your most sensitive data, including shared servers and cloud hosts.
Ask your developers or software providers how their applications clear sensitive data from memory after use.
Use platform features that isolate users and processes from each other, and avoid running sensitive workloads alongside untrusted ones.

requirements.title: Backups of data are created, protected, maintained, and tested

statement.text: Backups of data are created, protected, maintained, and tested

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Continuously back up critical data in near-real-time, and back up other data frequently at agreed-upon schedules

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Test backups and restores for all types of data sources at least annually

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Securely store some backups offline and offsite so that an incident or disaster will not damage them

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Enforce geographic separation and geolocation restrictions for data backup storage

editorial.question: Does your organization back up its important data on a set schedule, keep the backups protected, and test that it can restore from them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Backups are often the difference between a short disruption and permanent loss after ransomware, hardware failure, or human error. A backup that cannot be restored, or that attackers can encrypt too, offers little protection.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Critical data is backed up continuously or in near-real-time, and other data on agreed schedules. Backups are protected and maintained, some are stored offline and offsite with geographic separation so one incident or disaster cannot damage them all, and backups and restores are tested for every type of data source at a frequency you define, such as at least annually.
nextSteps: List your critical data and decide how often each type must be backed up.
Keep at least one backup copy offline and in a separate location.
Restrict who can change or delete backups.
Restore a sample of each type of data on a regular schedule and record the results.

requirements.title: Configuration management practices are established and applied

statement.text: Configuration management practices are established and applied

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Establish, test, deploy, and maintain hardened baselines that enforce the organization's cybersecurity policies and provide only essential capabilities (i.e., principle of least functionality)

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Review all default configuration settings that may potentially impact cybersecurity when installing or upgrading software

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Monitor implemented software for deviations from approved baselines

editorial.question: Does your organization set secure standard configurations for its systems, review default settings, and check that systems stay configured that way over time?
editorial.whyItMatters: Systems often ship with default settings and extra features that attackers know how to exploit. A known, hardened configuration reduces those weaknesses and makes unexpected changes stand out.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You establish, test, deploy, and maintain hardened baselines (approved secure configurations) that enforce your policies and enable only the capabilities each system needs. Default settings that could affect security are reviewed when software is installed or upgraded, and systems are monitored for deviations from their approved baselines.
nextSteps: Write down a secure baseline for each common system type, such as laptops, servers, network devices, and cloud accounts.
Change default passwords and turn off features and services you do not use.
Review security-related default settings whenever you install or upgrade software.
Check systems periodically, or with automated tools, for changes from the baseline.

requirements.title: Software is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk

statement.text: Software is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Perform routine and emergency patching within the timeframes specified in the vulnerability management plan

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Update container images, and deploy new container instances to replace rather than update existing instances

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Replace end-of-life software and service versions with supported, maintained versions

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Uninstall and remove unauthorized software and services that pose undue risks

examples.label: Ex5
examples.text: Uninstall and remove any unnecessary software components (e.g., operating system utilities) that attackers might misuse

examples.label: Ex6
examples.text: Define and implement plans for software and service end-of-life maintenance support and obsolescence

editorial.question: Does your organization keep software patched, replace versions that are no longer supported, and remove software that is unauthorized or unnecessary?
editorial.whyItMatters: Attackers routinely exploit known flaws in unpatched or unsupported software. Every unneeded program is one more thing to patch and one more tool an attacker could misuse.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Routine and emergency patches are applied within the timeframes in your vulnerability management plan, and container images are updated and replaced rather than patched in place. You plan for software end of life, replace unsupported versions with maintained ones, and remove unauthorized software and unnecessary components that attackers might misuse.
nextSteps: Turn on automatic updates where possible and set target timeframes for routine and emergency patches.
Identify software that is near or past its end of support and plan its replacement.
Remove unauthorized programs and unneeded components, such as utilities attackers could misuse.

requirements.title: Hardware is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk

statement.text: Hardware is maintained, replaced, and removed commensurate with risk

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Replace hardware when it lacks needed security capabilities or when it cannot support software with needed security capabilities

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Define and implement plans for hardware end-of-life maintenance support and obsolescence

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Perform hardware disposal in a secure, responsible, and auditable manner

editorial.question: Does your organization maintain its hardware, replace devices that can no longer support needed security features, and dispose of old equipment securely?
editorial.whyItMatters: Older devices may stop receiving security updates or lack features such as hardware encryption support. Discarded equipment can still hold data that someone else can recover.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Hardware is replaced when it lacks needed security capabilities or cannot run software that has them, and you have plans for end-of-life support and obsolescence. Disposal is secure, responsible, and auditable, with records showing how each device was handled.
nextSteps: Record the end-of-support dates for your computers, phones, and network equipment.
Budget and schedule replacements for devices that will lose security support.
Wipe or destroy storage before disposing of devices, and keep a record of what was disposed of and how.

requirements.title: Log records are generated and made available for continuous monitoring

statement.text: Log records are generated and made available for continuous monitoring

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Configure all operating systems, applications, and services (including cloud-based services) to generate log records

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Configure log generators to securely share their logs with the organization's logging infrastructure systems and services

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Configure log generators to record the data needed by zero-trust architectures

editorial.question: Do your systems, applications, and cloud services record activity logs and send them somewhere your organization can review them?
editorial.whyItMatters: Logs are often the only record of what happened during an attack. Without them, problems go unnoticed and investigations have little to work with.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Operating systems, applications, and services, including cloud services, are configured to generate log records. Those logs are shared securely with your logging infrastructure and include the data your monitoring needs, including what any zero trust architecture (an approach that verifies every access request rather than trusting the network) relies on.
nextSteps: List your important systems and cloud services and confirm logging is turned on for each.
Send logs securely to a central place where they can be reviewed and protected from tampering.
Confirm the logs capture key events, such as logins, administrator actions, and configuration changes.

requirements.title: Installation and execution of unauthorized software are prevented

statement.text: Installation and execution of unauthorized software are prevented

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: When risk warrants it, restrict software execution to permitted products only or deny the execution of prohibited and unauthorized software

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Verify the source of new software and the software's integrity before installing it

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Configure platforms to use only approved DNS services that block access to known malicious domains

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Configure platforms to allow the installation of organization-approved software only

editorial.question: Does your organization prevent people from installing or running software that has not been approved?
editorial.whyItMatters: Malware often arrives disguised as a useful program or browser add-on. Limiting what can be installed and run stops much of it before it starts.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Platforms allow installation of organization-approved software only, and where risk warrants, execution is limited to permitted programs or prohibited software is blocked. The source and integrity of new software are verified before installation, and devices use approved DNS services (the system that turns web addresses into network locations) that block known malicious domains.
nextSteps: Remove administrator rights from everyday user accounts so software installation goes through an approval step.
Keep a list of approved software and a process for requesting additions.
Use application allowlisting (permitting only approved programs to run) on high-risk systems.
Configure devices to use a DNS filtering service that blocks known malicious sites.

requirements.title: Secure software development practices are integrated, and their performance is monitored throughout the software development life cycle

statement.text: Secure software development practices are integrated, and their performance is monitored throughout the software development life cycle

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Protect all components of organization-developed software from tampering and unauthorized access

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Secure all software produced by the organization, with minimal vulnerabilities in their releases

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Maintain the software used in production environments, and securely dispose of software once it is no longer needed

editorial.question: If your organization develops software, does it build security into each stage of development and track how well those practices are working?
editorial.whyItMatters: Flaws introduced during development become vulnerabilities in what you release or run. Tampering with source code or build tools can slip malicious code into software you and your customers trust.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Secure development practices are integrated into every phase of the software development life cycle, and their performance is monitored. All components of your software are protected from tampering and unauthorized access, releases have minimal vulnerabilities, production software is maintained, and software that is no longer needed is securely disposed of.
nextSteps: Restrict and log access to source code, build systems, and release processes.
Add security reviews and automated vulnerability testing before each release.
Track measures, such as vulnerabilities found before and after release, to see whether your practices are working.
Retire and securely remove software you no longer maintain.

requirements.title: Networks and environments are protected from unauthorized logical access and usage

statement.text: Networks and environments are protected from unauthorized logical access and usage

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Logically segment organization networks and cloud-based platforms according to trust boundaries and platform types (e.g., IT, IoT, OT, mobile, guests), and permit required communications only between segments

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Logically segment organization networks from external networks, and permit only necessary communications to enter the organization's networks from the external networks

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Implement zero trust architectures to restrict network access to each resource to the minimum necessary

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Check the cyber health of endpoints before allowing them to access and use production resources

editorial.question: Does your organization separate its networks by trust level and limit what traffic can enter from the internet or move between network segments?
editorial.whyItMatters: On a flat network, an attacker who compromises one device can reach everything else. Segmentation and tight access rules contain that spread and keep untrusted devices away from important systems.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Networks and cloud platforms are logically segmented by trust boundaries and platform types, such as office IT, internet of things devices, operational technology, mobile, and guest networks, with only required communications allowed between segments. Only necessary traffic enters from external networks, network access to each resource is limited to the minimum needed, and the health of endpoints is checked before they can use production resources.
nextSteps: Put guest Wi-Fi and smart devices, such as cameras and printers, on networks separate from business systems.
Review firewall rules and close inbound access that is not needed.
Limit which users and devices can reach each important system.
Check that devices are patched and protected before they can connect to sensitive resources.

requirements.title: The organization's technology assets are protected from environmental threats

statement.text: The organization's technology assets are protected from environmental threats

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Protect organizational equipment from known environmental threats, such as flooding, fire, wind, and excessive heat and humidity

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Include protection from environmental threats and provisions for adequate operating infrastructure in requirements for service providers that operate systems on the organization's behalf

editorial.question: Is your organization's equipment protected from environmental threats such as fire, flooding, wind, heat, and humidity, including at providers that run systems for you?
editorial.whyItMatters: A burst pipe, overheated server closet, or fire can take systems offline as surely as an attack. Providers that host your systems face the same risks.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Equipment is protected against the environmental threats known for its location, such as flooding, fire, wind, and excessive heat and humidity. Requirements for service providers that operate systems on your behalf include protection from environmental threats and adequate operating infrastructure, such as power and cooling.
nextSteps: Walk through the spaces where equipment sits and note risks such as water pipes, poor ventilation, or flood exposure.
Add protections that fit those risks, such as raised mounting, temperature monitoring, or fire suppression.
Include environmental protection and adequate power and cooling in your requirements for hosting and service providers.

requirements.title: Mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations

statement.text: Mechanisms are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Avoid single points of failure in systems and infrastructure

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Use load balancing to increase capacity and improve reliability

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Use high-availability components like redundant storage and power supplies to improve system reliability

editorial.question: Has your organization built redundancy into critical systems so they keep running in normal conditions and during disruptions, such as a failed component?
editorial.whyItMatters: If one server, internet connection, or power supply is all that keeps a critical service running, a single failure becomes an outage. Redundancy lets operations continue while the problem is fixed.
editorial.doneLooksLike: You know the resilience requirements for your critical systems and have mechanisms that meet them in both normal and adverse situations. Single points of failure are avoided, and measures such as load balancing (spreading work across several systems), redundant storage, and redundant power supplies are used where needed.
nextSteps: Identify single points of failure in your critical systems, including internet connections, power, and key servers.
Add redundancy where an outage would be most costly, such as a second internet connection or a backup power supply.
Confirm that backup components take over as expected when a primary component fails.

requirements.title: Adequate resource capacity to ensure availability is maintained

statement.text: Adequate resource capacity to ensure availability is maintained

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Monitor usage of storage, power, compute, network bandwidth, and other resources

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Forecast future needs, and scale resources accordingly

editorial.question: Does your organization monitor the storage, computing, power, and network capacity its systems use, and add resources before shortages affect availability?
editorial.whyItMatters: Running out of disk space, bandwidth, or computing power can bring services down without any attacker involved. Spare capacity also helps systems absorb sudden spikes in demand.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Use of storage, power, compute, network bandwidth, and other resources is monitored. You forecast future needs and scale resources so that availability is maintained.
nextSteps: Set alerts for storage, bandwidth, and computing use that approach their limits.
Review usage trends periodically and forecast what you will need next.
Plan upgrades or scale cloud resources before limits are reached.

requirements.title: Potentially adverse events are analyzed to better understand associated activities

statement.text: Potentially adverse events are analyzed to better understand associated activities

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use security information and event management (SIEM) or other tools to continuously monitor log events for known malicious and suspicious activity

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Utilize up-to-date cyber threat intelligence in log analysis tools to improve detection accuracy and characterize threat actors, their methods, and indicators of compromise

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Regularly conduct manual reviews of log events for technologies that cannot be sufficiently monitored through automation

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Use log analysis tools to generate reports on their findings

editorial.question: Does your organization analyze security logs and alerts, with tools or by hand, to understand what is happening when suspicious activity appears?
editorial.whyItMatters: Logs and alerts only help if someone or something examines them. Analysis turns a stream of events into an understanding of whether something malicious is under way.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Log events are monitored continuously for known malicious and suspicious activity using a security information and event management (SIEM) system or other tools, informed by current threat intelligence. Logs from technologies that automation cannot cover well are reviewed manually on a regular basis, and analysis tools produce reports on their findings.
nextSteps: Decide which logs matter most, such as email, login, firewall, and endpoint protection logs.
Use a monitoring tool or service to watch those logs for suspicious activity.
Schedule manual reviews for systems that automated tools cannot monitor well.
Keep reports of findings so you can spot trends and follow up.

requirements.title: Information is correlated from multiple sources

statement.text: Information is correlated from multiple sources

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Constantly transfer log data generated by other sources to a relatively small number of log servers

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Use event correlation technology (e.g., SIEM) to collect information captured by multiple sources

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Utilize cyber threat intelligence to help correlate events among log sources

editorial.question: Does your organization bring together information from multiple sources, such as logs from different systems, to see connections between related events?
editorial.whyItMatters: A single login, file change, or network connection can look harmless on its own. Seen together across systems, the same events can reveal an attack in progress.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Log data from your various sources flows continuously to a small number of log servers. Event correlation technology, such as a SIEM (a system that collects and analyzes security events), links information captured by multiple sources, and threat intelligence helps connect events across those sources.
nextSteps: Send logs from your key systems and cloud services to one central location.
Use a tool or service that can correlate events across those sources.
Add threat intelligence feeds so related activity can be linked to known attack patterns.

requirements.title: The estimated impact and scope of adverse events are understood

statement.text: The estimated impact and scope of adverse events are understood

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use SIEMs or other tools to estimate impact and scope, and review and refine the estimates

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: A person creates their own estimates of impact and scope

editorial.question: When a potentially harmful event is detected, does your organization estimate how far it reaches and how much it could affect the business?
editorial.whyItMatters: Knowing whether an event touches one laptop or the whole network shapes how urgently and how broadly you respond. Underestimating scope can leave part of a problem unaddressed.
editorial.doneLooksLike: For adverse events, you estimate impact and scope, either with tools such as a SIEM or through a knowledgeable person's own assessment. Those estimates are reviewed and refined as more is learned.
nextSteps: Define a few impact levels based on which systems, data, and customers are affected.
Assign someone to estimate impact and scope when a significant event is detected.
Revisit the estimate as the analysis progresses and record how it changed.

requirements.title: Information on adverse events is provided to authorized staff and tools

statement.text: Information on adverse events is provided to authorized staff and tools

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Use cybersecurity software to generate alerts and provide them to the security operations center (SOC), incident responders, and incident response tools

examples.label: Ex2
examples.text: Incident responders and other authorized personnel can access log analysis findings at all times

examples.label: Ex3
examples.text: Automatically create and assign tickets in the organization's ticketing system when certain types of alerts occur

examples.label: Ex4
examples.text: Manually create and assign tickets in the organization's ticketing system when technical staff discover indicators of compromise

editorial.question: When security tools detect something concerning, do the alerts reach the right people and systems, and can responders see analysis findings whenever they need them?
editorial.whyItMatters: An alert that sits unread in a console protects no one. Getting findings to the right people quickly is what makes detection useful.
editorial.doneLooksLike: Security software generates alerts and delivers them to your security operations center (SOC), incident responders, or response tools. Authorized responders can access log analysis findings at all times, and tickets are created and assigned automatically for certain alerts and manually when staff discover indicators of compromise (signs that a system has been breached).
nextSteps: Decide who receives each type of security alert, including any outside provider that monitors for you.
Route alerts into a ticketing system or tracked queue so each one is assigned an owner.
Confirm that responders can reach log findings outside business hours.

requirements.title: Cyber threat intelligence and other contextual information are integrated into the analysis

statement.text: Cyber threat intelligence and other contextual information are integrated into the analysis

examples.label: Ex1
examples.text: Securely provide cyber threat intelligence feeds to detection technologies, processes, and personnel

examples.label: Ex2
